knowledgePoints.name: The full inventory
knowledgePoints.teach:
Context is everything Claude sees on a turn:

  • the system prompt,
  • the message history,
  • tool definitions and tool results,
  • attached files and skills,
  • thinking blocks.

The two people forget are tool definitions and thinking blocks, because neither appears in the conversation as a user would read it. Twenty tools with four-sentence descriptions is a fixed cost on every single request.

You pay for all of it, in and out. Once the window is full, the request fails — it does not silently truncate.

The goal is to fit the right things in, not everything.

questions.q: Which of these occupies the context window?
options: System prompt, message history, tool definitions and results, attached files and skills, thinking blocks
Message history and system prompt only
Everything except tool definitions, which are processed separately
questions.explain: All of it. Tool definitions in particular are a fixed cost people routinely overlook.

questions.q: What happens when the context window fills?
options: The oldest turns are dropped automatically
The response is truncated with stop_reason max_tokens
Claude summarises the history on its own
questions.explain: It fails. Automatic summarisation is compaction, which is an opt-in you have to ask for.

reviewQuestions.q: How does the course state the goal of context management?
options: Fit the right things in, not everything
Keep every request under half the window
reviewQuestions.explain: Selection, not compression. Cost is a consequence; relevance is the objective.

knowledgePoints.name: A pattern, not a parameter
knowledgePoints.teach:
Just-in-time context is a design pattern, not an API feature. There is no field to set.

The move: don't preload everything. Load what is needed now, and let the agent pull more through tools when it asks.

PreloadedJust-in-time
the entire building code pasted into the system prompta lookup_building_code tool the agent calls when a question needs it

Note the dependency this creates: the pattern only works if the agent actually reaches for the tool, which makes it a tool description problem. A perfect just-in-time architecture with a vague description is an agent answering from nothing.

Of Anthropic's four context-management patterns this is the only one that is purely architectural. The other three — compaction, caching, memory — all have a request field or an implementation behind them.

questions.q: A 200-page manual sits in your system prompt “just in case”. What replaces it?
options: Server-side compaction, which will summarise it
A lookup tool the agent calls when a question needs the manual
A cache breakpoint after the manual
questions.explain: Just-in-time: don't preload, let the agent pull. Caching would make re-sending it cheaper without making it necessary.

questions.q: What makes just-in-time different from the other three context patterns?
options: It is the only one that reduces cost
It is a design pattern with no API feature behind it
It only applies to agents, not to workflows
questions.explain: Nothing to switch on. It is a decision about architecture.

reviewQuestions.q: Your just-in-time design is sound but the agent answers without ever calling the lookup tool. Where is the fault?
options: The context window is too small
The tool description — Claude reads it to decide whether to call the tool
The tool schema is too complex
reviewQuestions.explain: The pattern depends on the agent choosing to pull, and that choice is made from the description.

knowledgePoints.name: Let the API do the summarising
knowledgePoints.teach:
Opt in on the request:

"context_management": {"edits": [{"type": "compact"}]}

Once input crosses a trigger threshold, the API automatically summarises older turns. What that takes off your plate is the bookkeeping: you stop tracking conversation length, stop deciding when to trim, and stop writing the summarisation call yourself.

Compaction manages the conversation you already have. It does not decide what to load in the first place.

That is the line between it and just-in-time, and the two compose: pull data on demand, and compact the history of having pulled it.

Managed agents ship with compaction — and caching — on by default.

options: context_management with an edits entry of type compact
A cache_control block of type compact

questions.q: What does compaction take off your plate?
options: Deciding what to load into context in the first place
Tracking conversation length and deciding when to summarise
questions.explain: The bookkeeping. What to load is a different problem, and just-in-time's.

reviewQuestions.q: Which context features do managed agents enable by default?
reviewQuestions.explain: Both, since a hosted long-running loop needs them almost by definition.

knowledgePoints.name: Nothing is cached until you say so
knowledgePoints.teach:
Caching is not automatic. You add a breakpoint by hand.

You mark a block using its longhand form:

"system": [{
  "type": "text",
  "text": long_stable_instructions,
  "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}     # ← the breakpoint
}]

Then:

Everything before and including the breakpoint gets cached. Content after it is processed normally.

So the breakpoint is a prefix marker, not a tag on one block. Placing it after your tool definitions caches the tools and everything ahead of them; placing it at the end of the system prompt caches the tools and the system prompt both.

Best candidates are the things that rarely change: system prompts and tool definitions. The user's message, which is different every time, is not one.

questions.q: You put a cache breakpoint at the end of your tool definitions. What is cached?
options: Everything up to and including the tool definitions
questions.explain: A breakpoint caches the prefix — everything before and including it.

questions.q: Which parts of a request are the best caching candidates?
options: Tool results, which repeat across turns
questions.explain: Stability is the criterion, and those two rarely change.

reviewQuestions.q: Which block form is required to add a cache breakpoint?
options: The longhand block form, carrying cache_control
Either — cache_control is a top-level parameter
reviewQuestions.explain: cache_control hangs off a longhand block, so a plain string system prompt has to be rewritten as one.

knowledgePoints.name: The five numbers
knowledgePoints.teach:
RuleValue
Cache lifetimeone hour
Processing ordertools → system prompt → messages
Maximum breakpoints4
Minimum cacheable size1,024 tokens up to the breakpoint
Prefix matchidentical — byte for byte

Breakpoints can span multiple messages and types: text blocks, system prompts, tool definitions, image blocks, tool use and tool result blocks.

Two consequences worth holding:

  • The 1,024-token minimum is summed across everything up to the breakpoint, so a short “Hi there!” system prompt will not qualify no matter how often you send it.
  • The processing order is why tools are the natural first breakpoint: they are processed first, so they are the outermost prefix.

questions.q: Your cache never hits, though the system prompt is identical — except you now interpolate the user's first name at the top. Which rule did you break?
options: The requirement that the cached prefix be identical
questions.explain: The prefix must match byte for byte. A name at the top changes the very first thing processed.

questions.q: What is the processing order that caching follows?
questions.explain: Tools first, which is why they make the natural outermost breakpoint.

knowledgePoints.name: One hour, and why 'please' costs money
knowledgePoints.teach:
The cache lives one hour, so it only helps if you resend the same content inside that window. A batch job running nightly gets nothing from it; a chat service under steady load gets a great deal.

Follow-up requests only hit the cache if the content up to the breakpoint is identical. Adding “please” invalidates it.

That is the rule that catches people, because the changes that break it are ones that feel harmless: a timestamp in the system prompt, a personalised greeting, a version string, a reordered tool array. Each of them is a different prefix, and a different prefix is a cache miss on everything behind it.

The practical discipline: put everything volatile after the last breakpoint, and keep the prefix byte-stable even when it feels over-careful.

questions.q: How long does the cache live?
questions.explain: One hour. Useful only if you resend the same prefix within it.

questions.q: Which of these is safe for a cached prefix?
options: A timestamp at the top of the system prompt
The user's name interpolated into the system prompt
Volatile content placed after the last breakpoint
Reordering the tools array per request
questions.explain: After the breakpoint is the safe place for anything that changes. The other three all alter the prefix.

reviewQuestions.q: How many cache breakpoints may a request carry?
What is the minimum cacheable size, and how is it measured?
options: 1,024 tokens, measured on the marked block alone
1,024 tokens, summed across everything up to the breakpoint
512 tokens, summed across the whole request
reviewQuestions.explain: Summed across the prefix — which is why a breakpoint after a short system prompt can still qualify if tools precede it.

knowledgePoints.name: Context that outlives the session
knowledgePoints.teach:
Compaction and caching both operate on a conversation. Memory is for what must survive after it: preferences, running notes, anything you want available next week.

Claude reads and writes a memory directory through tool calls, and Anthropic auto-injects an instruction telling it to check memory before starting work.

You implement the storage backend — file system, database, whatever you run.

Same division as the text editor tool: the interface is supplied, the substance is yours. Which also means the retention policy, the access control, and the question of what happens when two sessions write at once are all yours.

questions.q: Your agent should remember a user's preferences next week. Which pattern, and what do you build?
options: Compaction; nothing — it is a request field
The memory tool; you build the storage backend
Prompt caching; you build a one-hour refresh loop
Just-in-time; you build a preferences lookup tool
questions.explain: Cross-session continuity is memory's job, and the backend is yours to implement.

questions.q: What does Anthropic inject automatically when the memory tool is in use?
options: An instruction telling Claude to check memory before starting work
A cache breakpoint before the memory directory
questions.explain: The check-memory-first instruction. Without it, memory that exists is memory that goes unread.

reviewQuestions.explain: In production you typically layer all four — cache the stable prefix, pull data just-in-time, compact the history, persist across sessions.
